the-name.body:
The name is attested in Chinese characters as **女媧**. Etymologically it means "Woman wa"[^1].

The ASCII form *nuwa* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Nǚwā** recovers both the stress accent and the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **n** → **N** — Same, capitalized
- **u** → **ǚ** — Stress on u
- **w** → **w** — Same
- **a** → **ā** — Long vowel

The project holds the domain **nǚwā.com** (xn--nw-ela08f.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Shanhaijing.
Huainanzi, Liu An; Chinese Text Project, 139 BCE.

overview.body:
**Nǚwā** (*nuwa*) — The Mender of the Sky — belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Creation, Mending Heaven". The name means "Woman wa"[^1].

Nǚwā is the great repairer: the goddess who melted five-colored stones to patch the broken sky, cut off the giant turtle's legs to prop the corners of the world, and — on a quieter day — knelt by the Yellow River and made the first human beings out of mud.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Nǚwā** and serves its temple at [nǚwā.com](https://xn--nw-ela08f.com). The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *nuwa* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Huainanzi, Liu An; Chinese Text Project, 139 BCE.
Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1993.
Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), Sima Qian; Chinese Text Project, 91 BCE.

original-script.body:
The name is written in Chinese characters as **女媧**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *nuwa* and the PuniCodex restoration **Nǚwā** are measured: the restoration preserves both its pitch accent and its vowel quantity of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.[^1]

Written 女娲: nǚ (woman) plus wā — a graph so specific to her that dictionaries list almost no other word under it. The ü of the restoration is the sound itself; without it, the name is another word.

sources.citation: Huainanzi, Liu An; Chinese Text Project, 139 BCE.

domains.body:
Nǚwā is the great repairer: the goddess who melted five-colored stones to patch the broken sky, cut off the giant turtle's legs to prop the corners of the world, and — on a quieter day — knelt by the Yellow River and made the first human beings out of mud.[^1]

### The Five-Colored Stones

Melted and poured into the sky's wound — the world's first and greatest repair.

### The Serpent Body

Her form in Han art: human head, serpent body — earth's maker in earth's image.

### The Rope of Mud

The rich she shaped by hand, the poor she flung from a rope — humanity's two fortunes.

### The Marriage Rites

She instituted marriage and is prayed to for children — society's first legislator.

sources.citation: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1993.

symbols.body:
The iconography associated with Nǚwā concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The five colors** — The five phases (wood, fire, earth, metal, water) — the sky rebuilt in cosmic order
- **The compass** — Her emblem in Han art, paired with Fúxī's square — heaven's measure in her hand
- **The turtle's legs** — The four pillars she cut and set — sacrifice repurposed as architecture

sources.citation: Huainanzi, Liu An; Chinese Text Project, 139 BCE.

mythology.body:
Nǚwā's two great myths answer the two great questions: where people came from, and why the sky holds. Both are told in the earliest strata of Chinese myth and never improved upon.[^1]

### The Mending of the Sky (The Catastrophe)

The Huáinánzǐ tells it: in high antiquity the four pillars snapped, the nine provinces split; fire raged unquenched, waters rose undrained; fierce beasts devoured the people. Nǚwā melted stones of five colors to mend the azure sky, cut the legs of the great turtle to set the four pillars, slew the black dragon to save Jì province, and heaped reed-ashes to dam the flood. Then — and only then — the world was habitable, and the beasts went quiet.[^2]

### People of Yellow Earth (The Creation)

The later compendia preserve the gentler myth: Nǚwā, walking alone in the empty world, knelt by the river and shaped human beings from yellow clay. The work delighted but wearied her — so she trailed a rope through the mud and flung the drops, which became people too. The handmade figures became the rich and noble; the rope-flung drops, the poor and common — China's oldest reflection on how inequality began.

### The First Matchmaker (The Institution)

Having made people singly, she made them continuous: Nǚwā instituted marriage and the go-between, so that humanity could reproduce itself without her kneeling by the river forever. She is therefore prayed to for children and for marriages — the goddess who outsourced creation to love. The tradition names her among the Three August Ones: progenitor, legislator, and engineer in one.

sources.citation: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1993.
Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), Sima Qian; Chinese Text Project, 91 BCE.

syncretism.body:
She pairs with Fúxī as sister-wife in the Han synthesis — their intertwined serpent bodies, compass and square in hand, form the canonical image of cosmic order — and she absorbs older creation figures as the myth spread south and north. Modern readers note her kinship with every world-mother from Gaia to the Navajo Changing Woman, but the Chinese tradition keeps her distinct signature: she is not just a mother but a repairer, the goddess of maintenance.[^1]

Within the Chinese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[bagua|Bāguà]], [[fuxi|Fúxī]], [[guanyin|Guānyīn]], [[long|Lóng]], [[mengpo|Méngpó]], and [[pangu|Pángǔ]].

sources.citation: Huainanzi, Liu An; Chinese Text Project, 139 BCE.

cultural-legacy.body: Her stones became literature: the great novel Dream of the Red Chamber (Hónglóu mèng) opens with the one stone Nǚwā rejected for the sky — the stone that becomes the hero's jade and the book itself. "Nǚwā mends the sky" is the standing idiom for heroic repair; engineers, surgeons, and diplomats are all praised with it. Temples to her survive across North China — Shexian's cliff-hanging Wahuang Palace in Hebei is the grandest — where she is still prayed to for children.[^1]

sources.citation: Huainanzi, Liu An; Chinese Text Project, 139 BCE.

archaeology.body:
The Wahuang Palace at Shexian — pavilions chained to a cliff above the Zhang River, founded in the Northern Qi dynasty (6th century) — is her principal surviving sanctuary and one of China's architectural marvels. Han pictorial stones pair her with Fúxī from Shandong to Sichuan; the Astana cemetery silk banner carried the image to the Silk Road's far end. Her myth's textual strata are mapped from the Huáinánzǐ (139 BCE) backward into Warring States fragments and forward into the Tang flood-cycle accounts.[^1]

The **Wahuang Palace at Shexian** (Hebei) is her architectural marvel: pavilions chained to the sheer cliff of Phoenix Mountain, founded under the Northern Qi (6th century) and rebuilt across fifteen centuries — the 'hanging temple of Empress Wa,' still crowded at her third-month festival. **Tianshui** in Gansu claims her birth beside Fúxī's, and the paired shrines of the two serpent-ancestors mark the silk-road towns westward. Han pictorial stones from **Shandong's Wu Liang shrine** to the Astana cemetery of Xinjiang show her with compass raised beside her brother-husband — the oldest surviving portraits of the mender.

sources.citation: Huainanzi, Liu An; Chinese Text Project, 139 BCE.
The Shexian Wahuang Palace records; Wu Hung, The Wu Liang Shrine.

meditation.body:
Nǚwā is the goddess of the second day — the one after the catastrophe. Creation, in her myth, is not a single word but a continuous mending: sky patched, pillars reset, people shaped and taught. She asks the question every survivor, every parent, every civilization must answer: the world broke once; what, with your own two hands, have you repaired?

The rope and the handmade figures remain the tradition's quiet self-critique: some are shaped with care, some flung from a rope — and the goddess who made both is the one who mends the sky for all of them. Repair is her gospel and her rebuke: the world will break — pillars snap, heavens leak — and the measure of the maker is not the first creation but the mending. She is, for every restorer, nurse, and engineer of last resort, the patron of the second day.[^1]

sources.citation: Huainanzi, Liu An; Chinese Text Project, 139 BCE.

classical-texts.body:
The repairer's titles are all honours of maintenance.

- **Wāhuáng (媧皇)** — 'Empress Wa'; her royal title in the temple liturgies.
- **Nǚwā niángniang** — 'Lady Nǚwā'; the vernacular title under which mothers pray to her.
- **Sānhuáng** — 'one of the Three August Ones'; her place in the succession.
- **Zào rén zhī mǔ** — 'Mother of Made Mankind'; the folk-title of the clay myth.
- **Bǔtiān zhī shén** — 'the Goddess Who Mended the Sky'; the title the idiom keeps.

sources.citation: Huainanzi 6; Birrell, Chinese Mythology (Nüwa traditions).

daoist-sources.body: Daoist registers place Wāhuáng among the high antiquity goddesses: the cosmological treatises pair her with Fúxī as the measure-bearers of the first order, and the inner-alchemical tradition reads the five-colored stones through the five phases (wǔxíng) — her repair of the sky as the cosmos' own elemental rebalancing. Temple registers of the integrated Three Teachings give her altars as the mender-mother, and the precious scrolls retell the sky-mending as a parable of restoration that the Daoist healing liturgies echo.

sources.citation: Daozang cosmological treatises; the baojuan sky-mending retellings.

buddhist-sources.body: Buddhist engagement with Nǚwā is peripheral but real: she enters the apologetic lists of Chinese sage-ancestors whom the dharma honors without absorbing, and popular Buddhist-Daoist-folk temples enshrine her beside Guānyīn as a merciful mother-power. The creation-from-clay and the sky-repair appear in vernacular Buddhist storytelling as illustrations of compassionate world-maintenance, the tradition borrowing her for the point that the world is kept by those who mend it.

sources.citation: The apologetic sage-king lists; syncretic temple registers.

calligraphy.body: 女娲: nǚ (女) is the kneeling-woman graph, among the oldest in the script; wā (媧) was made for her alone — woman-radical plus the phonetic 呙 — a character with essentially no other word to spell, which is itself a kind of monument. Seal-script forms of the pair appear in the Han stone tradition beside her serpent-bodied portraits, and the great calligraphy of the Wahuang Palace cliffs at Shexian keeps her name carved where her temples hang: the word and the shrine in one stone.

sources.citation: Shuowen Jiezi (女, 媧); the Shexian cliff inscriptions.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ny˨˩˦ wa˥/** — Mandarin (Hanyu Pinyin with tones).[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: nyoo-wah, low-dipping tone on Nǚ, high level on Wā.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Chinese** — 女媧
- **Her title** — 媧皇 (Wāhuáng)
- **Owned form** — Nǚwā

Nǚwā 女娲 bears the third tone on nǚ — the vowel ü written with its two dots, which the restoration keeps and plain ASCII drops. Wā is the level-toned archaic graph for this goddess alone: a character invented for her name, used for nothing else in the language. The ü is the front rounded vowel — the sound French writes u — which plain ASCII loses to plain u.

sources.citation: Huainanzi, Liu An; Chinese Text Project, 139 BCE.
